extracted.intended_audience: covered entities (health care providers, issuers/insurers, State Medicaid agencies and MCOs), health IT vendors, civil-rights advocates, and regulatory commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize the regulatory standards, prohibitions, and evaluative criteria in HHS OCR's final rule (responses to comments) implementing section 1557 nondiscrimination protections for health programs, with emphasis on coverage exclusions, gender-affirming care, abortion-related care, and the integration requirement for people with disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of medications/health services related to abortion may be discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying access to specific medication or health services that may potentially be used for medication abortion purposes but are prescribed for reasons unrelated to abortion care may constitute discrimination under section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR declined to add additional regulatory text specifically prohibiting such denials, but states the principle that these denials can violate section 1557; enforcement is fact-specific and will be assessed case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on simultaneous (intersectional) discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneous discrimination on multiple prohibited bases (e.g., sex and disability, race and disability) is important to account for and is prohibited by section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will consider intersectional claims and notes that allegations raising multiple protected bases should be accounted for in enforcement and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If coverage is offered it must be nondiscriminatory (abortion example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the rule requires any covered entity to provide abortions or any particular medical care; however, to the extent plans offer coverage for termination of pregnancies and related services, they must do so on a nondiscriminatory basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering coverage triggers nondiscrimination obligations for how that coverage is administered, priced, limited, or excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prohibition on discriminatory limitations (§92.207(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.207(b)(1) provides a general prohibition on discriminatory limitations, exclusions, and cost-sharing practices; it is not intended to list every potentially prohibited exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will apply the general prohibition to any exclusion or limitation that results in discrimination on the basis of sex (or other protected bases). OCR declines to enumerate every type of care in the regulatory text; instead, the general prohibition captures diverse types of potentially discriminatory exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on categorical exclusions for gender transition/gender-affirming care (§92.207(b)(3)-(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions in §92.207(b)(3)–(5) prohibit categorical coverage exclusions on gender transition or other gender-affirming care and prohibit discriminatory limits on such coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR recognizes the extensive discrimination faced by transgender and intersex people and will investigate exclusions or limitations on a case-by-case basis; OCR will not provide a regulatory definition of 'gender-affirming care' but treats categorical exclusions as presumptively problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure-specific 'cosmetic' exclusions and gender-affirming care
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying procedures as 'cosmetic' when they are needed for gender-affirming care can be contrary to standards of care and may effectively exclude necessary treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR declined to add explicit regulatory text banning 'cosmetic' exclusions but explains that §92.207(b)(5)'s general prohibition on discriminatory limits on gender-affirming care will reach narrower procedure-specific exclusions; enforcement and analysis will be fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-categorical denials require case-by-case analysis (not per se discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every denial of gender-affirming care is automatically discriminatory; OCR will consider claims of non-categorical denials on a case-by-case basis to determine whether they entail discrimination on the basis of sex (or other protected bases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If an insurance plan places restrictions on gender-affirming surgeries that are no more stringent than restrictions placed on other surgical care, those restrictions will not violate the rule. Covered entities have opportunity to provide legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible nondiscriminatory denials based on medical necessity/anatomy
rubrics_metrics.description: A nondiscriminatory determination that care is not medically necessary based on a patient's anatomy or medical need is permissible under §92.207(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example: Denying a prostate exam for a transgender man who does not anatomically have a prostate is permissible; in contrast, denying medically necessary preventive care for a transgender patient could violate the rule. OCR will evaluate whether medical necessity standards are being applied in a nondiscriminatory way and not as pretext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health records should separately identify gender identity and anatomy (recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR appreciates suggestions to work with ONC and EHR vendors to ensure options for separately identifying a patient's gender identity and anatomy to reduce risk of improper denials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While minimum standards for record systems are not set in this rule, OCR is committed to working with stakeholders to explore solutions; better records may reduce erroneous denials based on mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex/gender marker mismatches in claims processing assessed case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims processing procedures that automatically deny coverage because of perceived mismatch of sex or gender may be a form of impermissible sex discrimination, but OCR will not categorically state that every such mismatch denial is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will investigate complaints under §92.207(b)(3) on a case-by-case basis; repeated denials or denials causing undue delay could lead to a finding of prohibited discrimination. OCR references prior discussion in the 2016 rule preamble regarding computer systems and gender coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line for 'comparable treatments'—fact-specific analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When coverage for comparable treatments is relevant to discrimination analysis, OCR declines to define a bright line of how similar care must be to be considered comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will evaluate comparability based on many relevant factors in a case-by-case inquiry rather than a fixed test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration requirement for people with disabilities (§92.207(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.207(b)(6) clarifies the prohibition on benefit designs that do not provide or administer health insurance coverage or other health-related coverage in the most integrated setting appropriate to the needs of qualified individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR recognizes this encompasses benefit design and implementation and aims to prevent unnecessary segregation; the provision is informed by ADA and section 504 integration mandates and court guidance on risk of institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration obligation extends to benefit implementation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The integration prohibition applies to both benefit design and implementation mechanisms controlled by covered entities, such as utilization management, provider reimbursement, contracting to third parties, and quality measurement/incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR provided an illustrative (non-exhaustive) list: coverage, exclusions, formularies, cost sharing (copays/coinsurance/deductibles), utilization management practices, medical management standards (including medical necessity), provider network design, provider reimbursement, provider admission standards, contracted administration (e.g., PBMs), quality measurement and incentive systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost or convenience are not per se legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons; fundamental alteration defense applies
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR notes that institutional care is generally more expensive than community-based care and that increased cost alone is not necessarily a fundamental alteration; concerns related to cost can be raised through a fundamental alteration defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will consider fundamental alteration defenses in enforcement; the rule clarifies there's a high bar for fundamental alteration and that increased cost alone does not automatically justify segregation or discriminatory benefit design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior authorization/step therapy discriminatory if applied to community-only care
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring prior authorization, step therapy, or other utilization management for individuals accessing treatment in the community but not in an institution can constitute discrimination if the discrepancy results in unnecessary segregation or a serious risk of unnecessary segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR explains such practices can delay care and push individuals into institutional settings to access treatment more quickly; these practices are subject to case-by-case enforcement under the integration requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious risk of institutionalization is actionable under integration mandate
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557's incorporation of section 504's integration provision makes clear that serious risk of institutionalization is covered; the integration mandate applies to people at serious risk of segregation or institutionalization, not only those already institutionalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR and courts assess 'serious risk' with a fact-based inquiry; relief may be appropriate to prevent unnecessary institutionalization. OCR explicitly prohibits benefit design that results in a serious risk of institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: States' Medicaid programs: no duty to create wholly new benefits but must provide services nondiscriminatorily in integrated settings
rubrics_metrics.description: A State Medicaid program is not generally required to create a 'new' program, but when it chooses to provide a service it must do so in a nondiscriminatory fashion by ensuring access in the most integrated setting appropriate. Services previously only available institutionally may need to be offered in the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR clarifies that offering a community-based version of an institutional benefit is not necessarily a 'new service' for fundamental alteration analysis; Medicaid statutory requirements are distinct from section 1557 obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-the-home restrictions may unlawfully limit community access
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies limiting benefits solely for 'use-in-the-home' (e.g., oxygen, wheelchairs, durable medical equipment) may prevent access to the broader community and could violate the most integrated setting requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'in-the-home' restrictions are not statutorily required, covered entities must assess claims individually to determine if denial violates the integration requirement. Statutory homebound criteria still require individualized assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managed care and contracting arrangements must avoid unjustified segregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Large issuers and managed care entities that apply uniform coverage policies across multiple product lines could employ policies that do not adequately support community integration; contracting structures (MCOs, PBMs, third-party administrators) must be scrutinized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities designing contracts should examine capitation, reimbursement, quality measurement, and incentive structures to ensure they do not result in unjustified segregation or place people with disabilities at serious risk of institutionalization. States contracting with MCOs remain liable when MCOs discriminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge planning that funnels patients to segregated settings can violate integration requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospitals or acute care providers that routinely discharge people with disabilities to nursing homes, psychiatric residential treatment facilities, or other segregated settings without assessing home-based support or community referrals may violate the integration provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities are prohibited from planning, service system design, and service implementation practices that result in a serious risk of institutionalization or segregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimbursement rates and network adequacy considered methods of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reimbursement rates and network adequacy constitute program administration methods and are relevant factors in OCR's analysis of whether practices result in discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will consider reimbursement practices, rate-setting, network adequacy, and their impact on capacity to provide community-based services when evaluating complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR will evaluate legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons and pretext; denials must not be based on unlawful animus
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities may defend nondiscriminatory actions by proffering legitimate reasons; OCR will assess whether such reasons are pretext for discrimination. The rule's revised §92.207(c) states that a denial or limitation must not be based on unlawful animus or bias or constitute a pretext for discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining pretext OCR will consider whether denials are based on medical necessity standards or reasonable medical management techniques that are not discriminatory. OCR also notes that burden-shifting frameworks like McDonnell Douglas are not required to be the sole method of proof; direct evidence cases differ from circumstantial ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR may issue future guidance and coordinate with DOJ; fundamental alteration guidance anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested more guidance on remedies, fundamental alteration analysis, and how OCR will incorporate DOJ ADA integration guidance; OCR may consider future sub-regulatory guidance and partnership with DOJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR clarified it will consider joint guidance with DOJ but declined to incorporate the fundamental alteration defense into the regulatory text beyond the existing provisions; the availability of the fundamental alteration defense is clear as drafted and OCR will provide further clarification in guidance as appropriate.
